prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, and for its realisation at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B046 as the sole part, credited to Katori and Ye. Having read all eight statements and the chair's questions, I answer the chair's three B046 questions directly. (1) Room after 2005 and 2012: the comb is the counter and the single-ion work is control of one quantum system. The lattice clock rests on a different idea, that a magic wavelength cancels the light shift of the clock transition for neutral atoms held in a lattice in the Lamb-Dicke regime, so that very many atoms are interrogated at once with no recoil or Doppler broadening. That gives a stability that a single ion cannot reach in comparable time, and it opened many-body clock physics. Neither earlier prize covers this. (2) Timing: I do not think the committee should tie a physics prize to a metrological decision. The achievement is verified by clock-to-clock comparison between independent laboratories and species at the 10^-18 level, which is stronger evidence than a formal redefinition would add. I still list the redefinition as a reservation, but no longer as a reason to wait. (3) Credit: the citation should separate concept from realisation, and with this wording two names are defensible. Katori made the proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group drove the systematic uncertainty and stability records and the many-body clock work. I have not changed my mind about which candidate to put first; what the debate changed is that I now state the citation more precisely and treat B038 and B042 as ranked alternatives, not as co-equals.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is that a sceptic can still read the lattice clock as a very large advance within a line already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and I cannot fully rebut that, only argue that the magic-wavelength and many-atom confinement ideas are distinct. Second, two names leave out real contributions: Lemonde and the Paris group on early strontium clock work, Ludlow, Takamoto, Schmidt and the PTB groups. The three-name limit would allow a third name, but I cannot decide from the supplied record who it should be, and adding a name would weaken the clean two-name story, so I would keep two. Third, the pending redefinition of the second leaves some colleagues uneasy and I take that seriously, though I do not find it decisive.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether the prize should reward the idea (Katori) more than the record-setting realisation (Ye), since Ye's contribution was a long accuracy programme more than a separate invention.
responses.response: I partly agree and I think the citation should carry this distinction instead of hiding it. Ye's group did more than tune a known device: the control of collisional and lattice-induced shifts, the move to Sr at the 10^-18 level and the use of the clock as a many-body quantum system are scientific advances, not only engineering. But I would not call Ye a co-inventor of the magic-wavelength idea. My revised citation says 'invention' for the concept and 'realisation at the 10^-18 level' for the programme, which is how I would defend two names against the objection that one of them is only a precision record.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B038, arguing that a Z2 classification is a deeper organising principle than a record-setting instrument and that the 2016 overlap is not decisive.
responses.response: I agree that the Z2 classification is conceptually the deeper idea and I share his view that it is distinct from the 2016 prize, which was about topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall phases. My disagreement is on the credit chain. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation that Molenkamp's group observed, and the three-person limit leaves no way to include them without losing Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. A prize that is correct in its science but leaves out the proposer of the platform will be read as unfair. His point that an organising principle should count above an instrument is fair, but the lattice clock is not only an instrument: the magic-wavelength condition is also a concept. I keep B038 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B038 and would word the citation around the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation in HgTe quantum wells, and doubts that the lattice clock is a discovery in its own right.
responses.response: Danielsson's wording of the citation is the best available way to handle B038 and, if the committee moved there, I could support it. It does not solve the problem that the platform was proposed by others: the 2007 observation in HgTe followed from the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and a citation that speaks of 'first observation in HgTe' makes that omission more visible. On whether the lattice clock is a discovery, the prize is for discovery, invention or improvement, and an invention with a precise origin and independently verified performance qualifies. Nature confirmed the magic-wavelength condition in the same way it confirmed the spin Hall prediction, by many labs obtaining the predicted cancellation.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B042, pointing to a falsifiable prediction followed by discovery and a three-name configuration that needs no forced exclusion.
responses.response: I take the falsifiable-prediction argument and the clean three-name mapping seriously, and I have moved B042 into my alternatives after reading her case. My position on timing is unchanged: eight years after the 2018 experiments the pairing mechanism is still disputed, the phase diagram depends on the sample and twist-angle disorder, and Cao, Fatemi and the earlier continuum-model authors are outside the credit. The clock result can be checked by independent clocks against each other, and has been, whereas moire quantum materials are still settling. If a younger-field prize is wanted, I would prefer the committee to wait a few years for the mechanism than to reward it now.

responses.point: Kroll raises the Boulder proximity to Ye (his research stay in Hall's laboratory) and suggests the committee consider recusal regarding Ye; he also would not widen the credit beyond two names.
responses.response: I agree that the credit should not be widened beyond two names, and I think his Boulder disclosure is the kind of field proximity the committee can judge without recusal, since no collaboration with Ye is documented. I hold a similar proximity myself, as an atomic theorist, and I would handle both the same way: disclose, and let the committee weigh it. I would add that this argues for the committee to test the case on its scientific merits, since the B046 support is not confined to one member or one subfield, with Johansson and Olsson reaching it from circuit QED and microscopy backgrounds.

responses.point: Olsson cautions that a 2026 precision-measurement prize follows the 2025 circuit-physics award, so the committee should not rotate toward the same quantum-technology community, and that Hall and Haensch and Wineland may reduce novelty.
responses.response: I think the 2025 point is weaker for B046 than for circuit QED. The 2025 prize concerned macroscopic quantum tunnelling in a superconducting circuit, whereas the lattice clock is atomic metrology with a different community, method and set of consequences (geodesy, constants, dark-sector searches). It would be a closer problem for B006, which is why I do not place it first. On Hall, Haensch and Wineland I agree that the novelty argument is the main one against B046, but I come out where she does: it is real, not decisive, because neither prize contains the magic-wavelength condition or the many-atom Lamb-Dicke confinement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the magic-wavelength and many-atom confinement ideas distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes; I cannot settle this from the supplied record.

Whether two names fairly represent the early strontium work (Lemonde and the Paris group, Ludlow, Takamoto, Schmidt and PTB), and whether the credit split between concept (Katori) and realisation (Ye) will survive scrutiny.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay the prize; I lean against waiting but hold this with less certainty than my view on the science.
I am relying on recollection of achieved clock uncertainties and have not verified current record values from the supplied evidence.
Whether a B038 citation can be framed so that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is acceptable.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: no direct connection to Katori or Ye is documented in my profile, and I have not seen anything in the round-1 statements that changes this. I work as a theorist in neighbouring atomic physics, and my documented collaborations (Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's ETH group, Reinhold Schuch, J. Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato) involve none of the credited names in B046, B038 or B042. I have no specific conflict for those entries and would not recuse myself, but I flag the field closeness for the committee to judge, as Kroll did for his own Boulder proximity.
